summary: Describes a way for one router to share circuits among several IS-IS routing protocol instances. Each instance forms its own adjacencies and can support multiple topologies, which isolates resources between instances. It was replaced by RFC 8202.

eli5.summary: One road with several separate bus lines running on it. Each line has its own drivers and stops, and they do not get in each other's way.

questions: how to run multiple is-is instances on one router
subtitle: Allows one router to run multiple independent IS-IS routing instances on the same physical link.

tldr.problem: IS-IS is a routing protocol used by Internet service providers, but the original design allowed only one instance per circuit, preventing flexible isolation of routing resources and topologies.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6822 adds a new Type-Length-Value field (Instance Identifier TLV) to IS-IS protocol data units, allowing routers to label traffic with an instance number and supporting multiple adjacencies and topologies per instance.
tldr.outcome: Multiple IS-IS instances can now share the same physical link without interfering with each other, enabling new deployment models for multi-tenant networks and application-specific routing. RFC 8202 later refined this mechanism.

today: RFC 6822 was replaced by RFC 8202, which provides clarifications and enhancements to multi-instance IS-IS. RFC 6822 remains the foundational specification for this feature in many deployed networks.

sections.title: IS-IS and the Single-Instance Limitation
sections.content:
IS-IS is a routing protocol used by many Internet service providers to exchange information about network topology. Before this RFC, IS-IS allowed only one instance to operate on any circuit (physical link). A circuit is the connection between two routers. If you wanted to run two separate routing domains on the same physical link, you would have needed two separate circuits or two separate routers.

This limitation became problematic for operators who wanted to isolate routing resources. For example, a provider might want to use one IS-IS instance for customer traffic and another for internal management, or run multiple virtual networks that do not interact. RFC 6822 removes this restriction, allowing multiple IS-IS instances to coexist on a single physical circuit while maintaining separate adjacencies, topologies, and Link State Databases (LSDBs).
sections.eli5: Before this RFC, you could only have one routing network per physical wire. Now you can have many independent routing networks on the same wire, and they do not talk to each other or get confused.

sections.title: Instance Identifiers and Topology Identifiers
sections.content:
The core mechanism is a new Instance Identifier TLV (Type-Length-Value field) added to every IS-IS protocol data unit (PDU) that belongs to a non-standard instance. The Instance Identifier (IID) is a 16-bit number that uniquely identifies which IS-IS instance a PDU belongs to. IID #0 is reserved for the standard instance—the original single instance that legacy routers understand.

Within a non-zero instance, the RFC supports multiple topologies. Each topology is identified by an Instance-Specific Topology Identifier (ITID)—another 16-bit number. Each topology has its own Link State Database and runs its own routing calculation, allowing a single instance to carry information for multiple independent networks. For example, one ITID might carry IPv4 routes while another carries IPv6 routes, and a third carries application-specific information without affecting the routing calculations of the others.
sections.eli5: The IID is like the license plate color: red plates for one business, blue plates for another. Within each business, the ITID is like a department: one drives customers, another handles packages. All on the same road without interfering.

sections.title: Instance Adjacencies and Routing
sections.content:
When two routers establish a connection using IS-IS, they exchange Hello PDUs to announce their presence. With multi-instance IS-IS, each router announces which instances and topologies it supports in the Hello. Two routers form an instance-specific adjacency: a link in the network graph that belongs to exactly one instance. If both routers support instances 1 and 2, they form two separate adjacencies—one for instance 1, one for instance 2—even though they are connected by the same physical link.

Each instance runs its own Update Process, which floods Link State PDUs and computes the shortest-path tree for routing. On point-to-point links, each instance independently discovers and maintains its own adjacencies. On broadcast links (like Ethernet), routers elect a Designated Intermediate System (DIS) per instance, and that DIS generates pseudo-node LSPs for each instance independently. The result is that traffic for instance 1 may follow a completely different path than traffic for instance 2, even on the same physical network.
sections.eli5: Each instance has its own team of routers who know each other and figure out the best paths for their traffic. They do not look at each other's maps or ask each other for directions.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility with Legacy Routers
sections.content:
The extension maintains backward compatibility. Legacy routers that do not support RFC 6822 ignore the Instance Identifier TLV and treat all PDUs as belonging to IID #0, the standard instance. To prevent confusion, MI-RTRs (Multi-Instance-capable routers) use different multicast addresses on broadcast circuits: the standard IS-IS addresses (AllL1IS, AllL2IS) for IID #0 PDUs, and two new dedicated multicast addresses (AllL1MI-ISs, AllL2MI-ISs) for non-zero IID PDUs. This way, legacy routers never see PDUs they do not understand.

On point-to-point circuits, MI-RTRs detect whether a neighbor supports the extension by checking for the presence of the IID-TLV in received Hellos. If a neighbor does not send an IID-TLV, it is a legacy router, and the MI-RTR avoids sending PDUs for non-zero instances on that link, preventing disruption. This allows operators to gradually deploy multi-instance IS-IS without requiring a flag-day upgrade of all routers.
sections.eli5: Old routers can still use the road, but they only see buses on the main (IID #0) line. Routers updated to support multiple lines know to separate the bus lines at different pickup points so the old routers never see mixed signals.

sections.title: Use Cases and Deployment Guidelines
sections.content:
Multiple IS-IS instances support diverse deployment models. A common pattern is one-to-one mapping: a single topology within a single instance, shared by multiple routers. This works well for simple isolation. When more granularity is needed, operators use many-to-one mapping: multiple topologies within one instance, each carrying information for a subset of routers. For example, routers that support video streaming use one ITID, routers supporting VoIP use another, and they maintain separate LSDBs.

The RFC recommends starting with a single non-zero instance to support multiple applications and topologies. Only when the set of topologies for one application group is largely disjoint from another should operators consider using multiple instances. Each instance consumes resources in the router's memory and CPU, so excessive instances degrade performance. The standard instance (IID #0) remains available for backward compatibility and can coexist with non-zero instances.
sections.eli5: You can organize the buses in many ways: all routes in one system, or some routes in system 1 and others in system 2 if they are very different. But too many separate systems makes the dispatcher's job harder.
